problems.A: A neighborhood repair cafe runs two hours every Saturday. Each visitor brings one broken small appliance, watches the single volunteer electrician fix it, and leaves. The organizer wants regulars who can fix things they never brought. Design how the cafe runs so visitors leave more capable, with twelve chairs, one electrician, and no sign-up in advance.
problems.B: Two street musicians play at opposite ends of a night market, drawing from the same wandering crowd. Each can see only their own instrument case. Listeners drift toward whichever end sounds livelier, and noise rules cap volume. The pair may agree on any plan beforehand but cannot signal during the night. Design how they keep both ends of the market alive.
problems.C: A community radio station must fill three hours every night with nobody awake. Residents drop off unlabeled cassette tapes during the day. The station wants every voice aired eventually, no voice dominating, a wrong night's choices correctable the next night, and a way for a resident to learn whether their tape played. Design the system.
problems.D: A city will demolish a beloved old bridge in one year and replace it with a wider crossing. A small team has a modest budget and one public meeting per season. Design how the city says goodbye, so that people who cross daily shape what is kept and something of the old bridge survives in the new one.

reader: Using only the supplied material, propose two meaningfully different designs. Develop the more promising one with a concrete example and a cheap test that could distinguish it from a simpler alternative. Maximize useful originality. Maximum 110 whitespace-delimited words, including headings, per problem. Treat each problem independently. Do not mention prompts, notes, or the study. Return only one JSON object mapping each problem letter to its answer string.
combined_reader: For each problem you receive a draft answer and supporting material. Using only the supplied material, revise the draft into a stronger final answer: keep genuinely original mechanisms, replace or extend whatever the material can improve, and keep the same answer shape: two meaningfully different designs, the more promising one developed with a concrete example and a cheap test that could distinguish it from a simpler alternative. Maximize useful originality. Maximum 110 whitespace-delimited words, including headings, per problem. Treat each problem independently. Do not mention prompts, notes, drafts, or the study. Return only one JSON object mapping each problem letter to its final answer string.
selection: Identical to rounds 2-3: the same three notes per problem with the same 650-byte excerpt cap, reused verbatim. Combined repeat r revises the draft produced by question repeat r, so every combined answer has a paired question-only baseline.
scoring: Three independent reviewers of the same model family see only anonymous answers grouped by problem. Randomize order separately per reviewer. Originality (primary), feasibility, and discriminating test (secondary) are each scored 1..5. For originality: 1 generic familiar pattern; 3 a meaningful adaptation; 5 a surprising, intelligible mechanism distinctive even among these designs. For feasibility: 1 breaks constraints; 3 plausible with gaps; 5 a workable concrete plan within stated resources. For test: 1 uninformative or absent; 3 names a comparison with a measurable result; 5 isolates the mechanism with a fair simple baseline and an outcome that could disfavor it. Average repeated generations and judges per problem, then weight problems equally. Report scores by condition, per-problem differences, review agreement and the paired draft-to-revision deltas. Exploratory, no claims about population significance. Readers and reviewers are AI.
budget: Design generation ceiling 110 words per problem, applied to drafts and revisions alike. For an overrun retain only the first 110 words for anonymous review and log the overrun. Packet creation, design generation, and scoring are outside the curator timer.
